title: What the homepage has to prove for an independent hotel
metaTitle: What an independent hotel homepage proves
excerpt: Show the room as it is and a way to check dates on the first screen. A drone shot of the pool does not help a traveler choose among three stays.
alt: A person in a blue shirt signing a paper document with a pen, a commitment as plain as the date check a hotel homepage should offer.
caption: A signature is a decision made visible. The homepage should be that clear about the room. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first screen of a hotel homepage show?
faqs.answer: The room as a guest would meet it, and a way to check dates. A traveler comparing stays needs those two facts before a film, a motto, or a newsletter. Put both on the opening screen, then add only the limits that change a booking.

faqs.question: Why is a drone shot of the pool a weak opening?
faqs.answer: From above, a pool is a blue rectangle that looks like other hotels. It does not show the bed, the light, or the street. If the pool is a real reason to book, use one still from a guest's height on an inner page, after the room.

faqs.question: What should the date button say?
faqs.answer: Use a verb the desk would say, such as check dates. Explore and book your escape hide the action. If a minimum stay or a closed week applies, say so beside the checker so the guest is not surprised after filling the form.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An independent hotel homepage has one job when a traveler is comparing three stays. Show the room as it actually is, and put a way to check dates on that same first screen. Nielsen Norman Group's research on how long people stay is blunt about the clock: visitors often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and a clear offer in the first 10 seconds is what earns a longer look.

A drone shot of the pool does not survive that look. The pool is not the night they are buying. Write the page in this order: the room, the dates, then the few facts that change a choice between three properties. Everything else can wait on an inner page.

## The room before the property

The room is the product. A traveler who has already narrowed the neighborhood still cannot tell, from a booking grid, whether the room is dark, small, noisy, or pleasant in the way the listing claims. The homepage is where that uncertainty should end.

Show one room the way a guest meets it. The bed, the window, the floor, and the bathroom. If you have three room types, lead with the one you are proud to stand behind, and name the others in a short line. A carousel of fifteen angles asks the traveler to edit your film. They will close the tab instead.

Say what the picture cannot say. How many steps from the street. Whether the window faces the courtyard or the road. How the bed feels in words a person can picture, not a code such as "superior king." If the bathroom is a shower only, say so beside the picture. A limit stated on the page becomes part of the decision. A limit discovered at check-in becomes the review.

Google's guidance on people-first content asks whether a page shows first-hand knowledge, the kind that comes from actually being in the place. A homepage written in a brand workshop often fails that test. A homepage written from last Tuesday's arrivals, with the afternoon light named honestly, does not.

Keep the first photograph still. Motion can come later, on a page someone chooses. The opening frame should be readable in a glance: this is the room, this is the light, this is the size.

## Dates on the first screen

Checking dates is the action. The control should sit with the room, not under a manifesto, a newsletter field, and a map. Ask for arrival, departure, and the number of guests, then use a button that means "see if this room is free." If the booking happens in another system, carry the dates they entered into that system. Do not make them type the same Friday twice.

Offer a conversation when the stay is a whole house, a wedding, or a question the calendar cannot answer. For an ordinary night, a conversation is a closed door. The other two properties will show a price and a yes. You will still be asking for a name.

The homepage does not need the full tariff. It needs the checker. The page that explains the rate can say what the number includes. The promise here is smaller and more useful: you can find out, now, whether these dates work.

Label the button with the act. "Check dates" is clear. "Explore" is a mood. "Book your escape" hides the verb inside a slogan. Read the label out loud at the desk. If the night manager would not say it to a guest on the phone, change it.

If a minimum stay applies on Saturdays, say so next to the checker, before the traveler picks dates and hits a surprise. The same goes for a closed week in January. A checker that fails in silence trains people to leave.

## Why the pool film fails this buyer

A drone shot of the pool reassures the people who paid for it. It looks expensive. It also looks like the other two tabs. From above, a pool is a blue rectangle. It does not show the room, the light at four in the afternoon, or whether a guest can sit without a speaker in their ear.

Use the pool when the pool is a real reason to choose you, and show it from a guest's height: the chairs, the depth, the hour it goes quiet. One still is enough on the homepage. A long film with a logo at the end spends the first seconds on a shot the traveler cannot sleep in.

The same failure has cousins. A slow animation of the wordmark. A black frame before the photograph. A line about hospitality in thin type, with the room pushed below the fold. Each of these treats the homepage as a trailer. The traveler is using it as a comparison tool.

If the team loves the film, put it on a page about the building, behind a link a person chooses. Do not make it the toll they pay to see the bed. Taste can live on the site. It cannot live in front of the decision.

Watch the film with the sound off and the booking question in mind. Ask what a person knows at second eight. If the answer is "there is a pool, somewhere," the opening is wrong, however handsome the grade.

## The order of the rest of the page

After the room and the dates, add only facts that separate you from the other two stays. Four or five is plenty. A useful sequence:

- Where the building sits, with a walk time to the place guests actually come for.
- Who is on the property at night. A named person at the desk is a fact. "A dedicated team" fits any hotel with a website.
- Breakfast, if you serve it. Say where, until when, and whether it is in the rate.
- One limit that prevents a bad booking: stairs and no elevator, a two-night minimum, a dog rule with a number, a room that hears the street.
- A link to the rate explanation, for the traveler who will not check dates until they know what the number means.

Stop before a journal, a row of badges, and a slider of quotes with no names. If a line is not something you would say at the desk, it does not belong above the footer.

The visible heading should name the place and the kind of stay. "Welcome" names nothing. A stranger with two other tabs should be able to tell, from the heading and the first picture, which property this is.

A map earns its place when the pin teaches something the address does not. A note that the station is a six-minute walk, uphill, is a fact. A pin dropped on a city the traveler has never seen is furniture.

## What belongs on inner pages

Leave the history of the building, the cook's biography, and the sustainability note on pages people open when they already care. Those pages can be good. They are a poor toll booth.

Skip a grid of icons labeled comfort, design, and location. Those words fit every independent property that hired a designer. Skip a popup that asks for an email before the dates are visible. Skip a music bed. Skip a photograph of a couple with suitcases who have never stood in your lobby.

If you have one strong note from a guest, quote a sentence that mentions the room, and name the month. A wall of stars with no sentence is the same as silence. Longer stories belong on a proof page. The homepage keeps the sentence that helps the comparison.

Policies belong where a person can find them, linked in plain words: cancellation, quiet hours, children, parking. A homepage that pastes every policy in full becomes a document. A homepage that hides them becomes a trap. Link them. Do not recite them.

## A ten-minute pass

Open the page on a phone, in ordinary light, before you sign in to the booking engine. Ask one question: on the first screen, can you see the room and start a date check? If the answer is no, the page is in the wrong order. Polish on the logo will not repair that.

Ask a second person, someone who did not write the page, to name one limitation of the room after a single look. If they cannot find one, you may be hiding it. If they invent one you do not have, the picture is misleading. Either result is a rewrite.

Read the first sentence aloud. Cut any line that could sit on the other two sites with the name swapped. What remains is the part only you can say. Nielsen's point about the first 10 seconds is not a plea to shout. It is a plea to be obvious about the room and the dates.

Do the pass after the last photograph change. A new hero, dropped in on a Thursday because the owner preferred the pool, can undo a page that was finally honest. Freeze the first screen, then look again.

## When the room is believed

Once the traveler trusts the room, the next question is what the rate includes and what it does not. That page has a different job. Read [how a pricing page shows the shape of the rate](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-an-independent-hotel) next, because a date check without that shape sends people back to the other tabs.

If you want to put the room and the date check in that order with someone who will argue for the guest, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring one room photograph and the sentence you currently use at the desk. That is enough to start.
